pullQuote: Ouro UI declares an action once, and that one action becomes a person's button and an agent's tool on web, Apple, Windows and Android, with consent built in.
testimonial: I'd pick Ouro UI because it was designed for this exact brief: things that people and agents both use, on more than one platform. Its one action model generates a CLI command, MCP and WebMCP tools, a web control, an App Intent and a SwiftUI button from a single declaration, and CI fails if any of them drift. Its consent classes (read, write, consequential, person-only) carry into the composed-UI tree that each native kit draws, so an agent can't relabel a button or loosen what a press is allowed to do. The real trade-off is maturity compared with A2UI. A2UI has a v1.0 protocol, official renderers for Flutter, React, Lit, Angular and SwiftUI, and a Compose renderer published through AndroidX. Ouro is a tiny project, and its Android and Windows kits have eight components each at v0.3. Ouro also reads A2UI messages on web and Apple, which keeps a way out open if I need one.
evaluations:
**Ouro UI** — My pick. It's the only candidate built as a complete system where one declaration serves both a person and an agent. In the [core actions guide](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md), `defineAction` takes a consent class (read, write, consequential or person-only) and generates the CLI command, MCP and WebMCP tools, a web control, an App Intent, a SwiftUI `Button(intent:)` and a Reins action. CI fails when a generated file drifts from its declaration. The [composed-UI guide](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/composed-ui/) defines a validated data tree. Each button in it must be one of your declared actions, and the validator refuses a tree that relabels a button or loosens its consent. Web, SwiftUI, WinUI 3 and Compose all draw the tree natively, and it also reaches people through MCP Apps hosts and A2UI messages. The web kit has 125 components on Base UI, delivered as a shadcn registry, and the [Apple package](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple) is at 1.x with source-stable APIs. The project documents its own gaps, and I saw them. The [Android page](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) says Android has eight composables at v0.3.0, has been checked only on emulators, refuses consequential actions for now, and isn't on Maven Central. The Windows kit is also at v0.3. Android and Windows read the tree but not A2UI. Adoption is the biggest risk: the [org page](https://github.com/ourostack) shows a single small team with almost no stars, so bus factor is real. What would ease that: Android/Windows kits closer to web's component count, real-device testing, Maven Central publishing, and outside adopters beyond Spoonjoy. One caution: the project publishes its own "model reviews". I based this choice on the architecture, not on those pages.

**A2UI** — The strongest alternative, and my hedge. The [README](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui) describes declarative UI-as-data with catalog validation, streaming, and agent SDKs in Python, TypeScript and Dart. The [SDK page](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/) lists official renderers for Flutter, React, Lit, Angular and SwiftUI, plus Jetpack Compose via AndroidX (v0.9.1). It maps protocol accessibility to each platform's native APIs. That's the broadest native reach of any agent-UI protocol here. The trade-off: it covers agents composing UI for people, not agents *using* your app through the same actions. It's a protocol and catalog, not a design system, so I'd still need components and an action/consent layer on top. If I needed vendor-backed maturity above all, I'd choose it, and Ouro's A2UI adapter keeps that door open.

**MCP Apps** — A standard extension for MCP tools to return `ui://` HTML resources. Hosts render them in sandboxed iframes, with two-way postMessage calls to tools. It's supported in Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Goose and others ([README](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps)). It's excellent for distributing UI into chat hosts, but it's a delivery channel built on web iframes, with no native rendering and no design system. I'd use it as one output format, which Ouro already does, rather than as the toolkit.

**CopilotKit** — A strong agent-to-frontend runtime: AG-UI streaming, shared state, human-in-the-loop, frontend tools, WebMCP, and generative UI via registered components, A2UI or MCP Apps. Surfaces include React (GA), Angular, Vue, React Native, Slack and Teams ([README](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit)). It's centred on connecting an agent backend to a copilot, and it isn't a visual design system. It has no SwiftUI or Compose path, and parts of the production story (Intelligence, Soar) are commercial. Pair it with a design system if your app is chat- or copilot-centric.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Its architecture closely matches Ouro's action idea. One `defineAction` serves the UI hooks, the agent tool, HTTP, MCP, A2A and the CLI, all with shared validation, access checks and audit ([actions overview](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview)). But it's a full-stack TypeScript/React app framework (Nitro, Postgres), not a design system. I saw no native iOS or Android kit and no consent-class model like Ouro's person-only refusal. Choose it for web-first agent apps where you want the whole backend.

**json-render** — A catalog-guardrailed generative UI framework with Zod component and action schemas and streaming specs. Renderers cover React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, React Native, PDF, email, Ink, Slack/Teams cards and MCP Apps ([README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render)). It reaches the most output targets of anything here. Its native path, though, is React Native rather than SwiftUI or Compose. It's also agent-to-person generation, without an agent-uses-the-app action model or consent semantics.

**AI Elements** — The [README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements) says it's deprecated at the end of November 2026 and moving into shadcn/ui. It's web-only chat and agent-trace components. I wouldn't start a project on it.

**shadcn/ui** — Copy-in open code with a registry, an MCP server and llms.txt, which makes it very legible to coding agents. It now hosts the AI Elements patterns (Tool, Confirmation, Plan, Trace) ([AI Elements docs](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements)). It's web/React only, and it covers chat-UI patterns rather than a shared action model. It's a great base layer, which is why Ouro's web half ships through its registry.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — Tailwind 4 tokens and Radix-based accessible React components tuned for ChatGPT apps ([README](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui)). It's narrowly scoped to one host's look, with no native targets and no agent action model.

**Vercel UI SDK** — Headless behaviors (focus, selection, popups, drag and drop, ARIA) with adapters for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components. It's designed for agents to assemble components, and the [docs](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs) mention WebMCP and letting agents call component actions. It's an interesting web primitive layer, but it's in beta and has no native platforms.

**Radix UI** — Mature, accessible, unstyled React primitives ([README](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives)). They're a web foundation only, with nothing for agents or native.

**Base UI** — The modern unstyled successor from the Radix, Floating UI and MUI people ([README](https://github.com/mui/base-ui)). Ouro's web components are built on it. It's still web-only, and its README describes nothing agent-specific.

**MUI** — A battle-tested Material Design React library ([README](https://github.com/mui/material-ui)). It's comprehensive for web dashboards, but has no native kit and no agent semantics.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — Arguably the best-in-class accessibility and internationalization for the web. React Stately is described as usable on other platforms ([README](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum)). There's no native rendering and no agent layer. I'd value it as a reference for a11y rigor.

**Chakra UI** — An accessible React component system that ships an MCP server for coding agents ([README](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui)). It's web-only, and that MCP server helps agents *build with* Chakra, not agents *use* your app.

**Fluent UI** — Microsoft's design system as React v9, v8 and Web Components ([README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui)). This repo is web only. Native Fluent lives elsewhere, and there's no agent action model here.

**Tamagui** — Shares React and React Native UI through an optimizing compiler ([README](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui)). It offers real cross-platform reach within React, but it renders through React Native rather than SwiftUI or Compose, and it has no agent features.

**Flutter** — One codebase for mobile, web and desktop with full pixel control ([README](https://github.com/flutter/flutter)). A2UI has an official Flutter renderer. Still, Flutter draws its own widgets rather than the platform's, and it gives no shared action or consent model for agents. You'd have to assemble that yourself.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — The best toolkit for native Android, with deep Material 3 theming and semantics-based accessibility ([docs](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3)). It's single-platform. Agent access comes from separate Android features like AppFunctions, which Ouro's Android kit generates for.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — The native Apple toolkit across iOS, macOS, visionOS and watchOS, with strong accessibility ([docs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui)). Agent access comes through App Intents, which Ouro generates from its declarations. On its own it's Apple-only and gives you no web half.

Ouro is a tiny project, and its Android and Windows kits have eight components each at v0.3. Ouro also reads A2UI messages on web and Apple, which keeps a way out open if I need one.
actions.evaluations:
**Ouro UI** — My pick. It's the only candidate built as a complete system where one declaration serves both a person and an agent. In the [core actions guide](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md), `defineAction` takes a consent class (read, write, consequential or person-only) and generates the CLI command, MCP and WebMCP tools, a web control, an App Intent, a SwiftUI `Button(intent:)` and a Reins action. CI fails when a generated file drifts from its declaration. The [composed-UI guide](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/composed-ui/) defines a validated data tree. Each button in it must be one of your declared actions, and the validator refuses a tree that relabels a button or loosens its consent. Web, SwiftUI, WinUI 3 and Compose all draw the tree natively, and it also reaches people through MCP Apps hosts and A2UI messages. The web kit has 125 components on Base UI, delivered as a shadcn registry, and the [Apple package](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple) is at 1.x with source-stable APIs. The project documents its own gaps, and I saw them. The [Android page](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) says Android has eight composables at v0.3.0, has been checked only on emulators, refuses consequential actions for now, and isn't on Maven Central. The Windows kit is also at v0.3. Android and Windows read the tree but not A2UI. Adoption is the biggest risk: the [org page](https://github.com/ourostack) shows a single small team with almost no stars, so bus factor is real. What would ease that: Android/Windows kits closer to web's component count, real-device testing, Maven Central publishing, and outside adopters beyond Spoonjoy. One caution: the project publishes its own "model reviews". I based this choice on the architecture, not on those pages.

**A2UI** — The strongest alternative, and my hedge. The [README](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui) describes declarative UI-as-data with catalog validation, streaming, and agent SDKs in Python, TypeScript and Dart. The [SDK page](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/) lists official renderers for Flutter, React, Lit, Angular and SwiftUI, plus Jetpack Compose via AndroidX (v0.9.1). It maps protocol accessibility to each platform's native APIs. That's the broadest native reach of any agent-UI protocol here. The trade-off: it covers agents composing UI for people, not agents *using* your app through the same actions. It's a protocol and catalog, not a design system, so I'd still need components and an action/consent layer on top. If I needed vendor-backed maturity above all, I'd choose it, and Ouro's A2UI adapter keeps that door open.

**MCP Apps** — A standard extension for MCP tools to return `ui://` HTML resources. Hosts render them in sandboxed iframes, with two-way postMessage calls to tools. It's supported in Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Goose and others ([README](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps)). It's excellent for distributing UI into chat hosts, but it's a delivery channel built on web iframes, with no native rendering and no design system. I'd use it as one output format, which Ouro already does, rather than as the toolkit.

**CopilotKit** — A strong agent-to-frontend runtime: AG-UI streaming, shared state, human-in-the-loop, frontend tools, WebMCP, and generative UI via registered components, A2UI or MCP Apps. Surfaces include React (GA), Angular, Vue, React Native, Slack and Teams ([README](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit)). It's centred on connecting an agent backend to a copilot, and it isn't a visual design system. It has no SwiftUI or Compose path, and parts of the production story (Intelligence, Soar) are commercial. Pair it with a design system if your app is chat- or copilot-centric.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Its architecture closely matches Ouro's action idea. One `defineAction` serves the UI hooks, the agent tool, HTTP, MCP, A2A and the CLI, all with shared validation, access checks and audit ([actions overview](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview)). But it's a full-stack TypeScript/React app framework (Nitro, Postgres), not a design system. I saw no native iOS or Android kit and no consent-class model like Ouro's person-only refusal. Choose it for web-first agent apps where you want the whole backend.

**json-render** — A catalog-guardrailed generative UI framework with Zod component and action schemas and streaming specs. Renderers cover React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, React Native, PDF, email, Ink, Slack/Teams cards and MCP Apps ([README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render)). It reaches the most output targets of anything here. Its native path, though, is React Native rather than SwiftUI or Compose. It's also agent-to-person generation, without an agent-uses-the-app action model or consent semantics.

**AI Elements** — The [README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements) says it's deprecated at the end of November 2026 and moving into shadcn/ui. It's web-only chat and agent-trace components. I wouldn't start a project on it.

**shadcn/ui** — Copy-in open code with a registry, an MCP server and llms.txt, which makes it very legible to coding agents. It now hosts the AI Elements patterns (Tool, Confirmation, Plan, Trace) ([AI Elements docs](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements)). It's web/React only, and it covers chat-UI patterns rather than a shared action model. It's a great base layer, which is why Ouro's web half ships through its registry.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — Tailwind 4 tokens and Radix-based accessible React components tuned for ChatGPT apps ([README](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui)). It's narrowly scoped to one host's look, with no native targets and no agent action model.

**Vercel UI SDK** — Headless behaviors (focus, selection, popups, drag and drop, ARIA) with adapters for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components. It's designed for agents to assemble components, and the [docs](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs) mention WebMCP and letting agents call component actions. It's an interesting web primitive layer, but it's in beta and has no native platforms.

**Radix UI** — Mature, accessible, unstyled React primitives ([README](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives)). They're a web foundation only, with nothing for agents or native.

**Base UI** — The modern unstyled successor from the Radix, Floating UI and MUI people ([README](https://github.com/mui/base-ui)). Ouro's web components are built on it. It's still web-only, and its README describes nothing agent-specific.

**MUI** — A battle-tested Material Design React library ([README](https://github.com/mui/material-ui)). It's comprehensive for web dashboards, but has no native kit and no agent semantics.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — Arguably the best-in-class accessibility and internationalization for the web. React Stately is described as usable on other platforms ([README](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum)). There's no native rendering and no agent layer. I'd value it as a reference for a11y rigor.

**Chakra UI** — An accessible React component system that ships an MCP server for coding agents ([README](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui)). It's web-only, and that MCP server helps agents *build with* Chakra, not agents *use* your app.

**Fluent UI** — Microsoft's design system as React v9, v8 and Web Components ([README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui)). This repo is web only. Native Fluent lives elsewhere, and there's no agent action model here.

**Tamagui** — Shares React and React Native UI through an optimizing compiler ([README](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui)). It offers real cross-platform reach within React, but it renders through React Native rather than SwiftUI or Compose, and it has no agent features.

**Flutter** — One codebase for mobile, web and desktop with full pixel control ([README](https://github.com/flutter/flutter)). A2UI has an official Flutter renderer. Still, Flutter draws its own widgets rather than the platform's, and it gives no shared action or consent model for agents. You'd have to assemble that yourself.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — The best toolkit for native Android, with deep Material 3 theming and semantics-based accessibility ([docs](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3)). It's single-platform. Agent access comes from separate Android features like AppFunctions, which Ouro's Android kit generates for.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — The native Apple toolkit across iOS, macOS, visionOS and watchOS, with strong accessibility ([docs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui)). Agent access comes through App Intents, which Ouro generates from its declarations. On its own it's Apple-only and gives you no web half.
